The Stream brown frog (Rana sakuraii) is a medium-sized ranid endemic to Japan, with marked sexual dimorphism in adult size. Females of this species attain a maximum snout–vent length of 5 cm [Li = 5 cm], a dimension that reflects the selective pressures of fecundity in this oviparous anuran. In contrast, males reach a smaller ultimate body length, measuring approximately 4.8 cm [Li = approximately 4.8 cm], a pattern consistent with many temperate ranids where male–male competition for amplexus favours agility over sheer size. This dimorphism is accompanied by substantial differences in body mass. Adult females achieve an ultimate wet weight of 11.3 grams [Wwi = 11.3 grams], whereas males plateau at a lower asymptotic mass of 10.0 grams [Wwi = 10.0 grams]. These differences in body size and mass have direct implications for reproductive output; larger females can accommodate more eggs per clutch, contributing to the population's overall fecundity.

Reproductive traits in Rana sakuraii are tied closely to thermal conditions during the breeding season. At a water temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C], which is typical of the shaded mountain streams where this frog spawns, females lay a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year], with each clutch containing between 500 and 3000 eggs [N_R_i = each clutch containing between 500 and 3000 eggs]. This considerable range in fecundity likely reflects variation in female body size and local resource availability. The eggs themselves are relatively large, with diameters ranging from 3.1 to 3.6 mm, a feature that influences the size of the hatchlings. Newly emerged larvae, or yolk-dependent tadpoles, have a wet weight at birth of just 0.0197 grams [Wwb = 0.0197 grams], a mass that is consistent with the substantial yolk reserves needed to sustain the endotrophic phase before the onset of exogenous feeding.

Embryonic and larval development proceed at rates governed by ambient temperature. Eggs incubated at 18 °C [T = 18 °C] undergo eclosion after approximately 35 days [ab = approximately 35 days], a duration that is comparable to that reported for the common frog Rana temporaria under similar thermal regimes. Following hatching, the lecithotrophic tadpoles begin exogenous feeding after yolk absorption completion. The subsequent larval period, from hatching to metamorphic climax, lasts approximately 45.75 days  when larvae are reared at 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. At the conclusion of metamorphosis, the juvenile froglets measure about 0.8 cm , reflecting the allometric shifts and body plan reorganisation that occur during tail resorption and limb development. This relatively small size at metamorphosis places the young frogs at risk of desiccation and predation, favouring the occupation of moist microhabitats.

Sexual maturation in Rana sakuraii is a protracted process, occurring several years following metamorphosis. Under the thermal conditions typical of the species' montane habitat, which average approximately 18 °C [T = 18 °C] during the active growing season, juveniles attain puberty at about 1095 days after metamorphosis [tp = about 1095 days after metamorphosis]. This extended juvenile period is characteristic of ranids with relatively large adult body sizes, as it allows sufficient time for somatic growth and the deposition of fat reserves necessary to support the energetic demands of reproduction. The overall longevity of the species is similarly substantial; the maximum lifespan in the wild is estimated at 2920 days [am = 2920 days], a value that places Rana sakuraii among the longer-lived members of its genus at a temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C]. This extended lifespan, combined with delayed maturity, suggests a life-history strategy that prioritises adult survival and repeated breeding over early reproduction.

Field studies of Rana sakuraii have revealed interesting patterns in its population structure and habitat use. The species is found exclusively in cool, fast-flowing mountain streams with rocky substrates, where it breeds in shallow pools and backwaters. The maximum body length of adult females, recorded at 5 cm [Li = 5 cm], is consistent with the upper range reported for frogs in the genus Rana from Japanese montane habitats. Male frogs plateau at an ultimate body mass of 10.0 grams [Wwi = 10.0 grams], a value that is approximately 88 percent of the asymptotic female mass, reflecting the modest sexual size dimorphism characteristic of this ranid species. Gravid females carry an asymptotic body mass of 11.3 grams [Wwi = 11.3 grams], a value that reflects the substantial energetic investment in oocyte production prior to each breeding season. Males, which plateau at 4.8 cm [Li = 4.8 cm] in snout-vent length and a corresponding mass of 10.0 grams, exhibit robust body proportions well suited to streamside locomotion. The population dynamics of this frog are sensitive to changes in stream temperature and flow regime, making it a potential indicator species for the health of montane stream ecosystems in Japan. Conservation efforts must therefore consider the preservation of these cool-water habitats to ensure the continued viability of local populations.
